pass_rule: all core questions substantially correct in the learner's own words; stretch questions inform the grade, not the gate

questions.prompt: You have `ch := make(chan int)` and `buf := make(chan int, 2)`. For each one: when does a send block, and when does a receive block?
expected_points: unbuffered: send blocks until a receiver is ready and receive blocks until a sender is ready — a rendezvous that synchronizes both goroutines
buffered: send blocks only while the buffer is full, receive only while it is empty — two sends on buf succeed with no receiver, the third blocks
an unbuffered send returning proves the receiver has the value; a buffered send only proves it entered the queue

questions.prompt: Who is allowed to close a channel, and what happens on a receive from a closed channel versus a send to one?
expected_points: only the sender closes — a receiver closing would make the sender's next send panic
receive from a closed channel never blocks: buffered leftovers first, then zero values, with comma-ok reporting false once drained
send to a closed channel panics, as does closing twice
closing is an optional broadcast signal, not cleanup — unclosed channels are garbage collected fine

questions.prompt: In your pipeline each stage runs `defer close(out)` in its goroutine. What breaks, and how loudly, if one stage forgets it?
expected_points: the downstream range never terminates, so every stage after the gap blocks forever — a goroutine leak
termination normally cascades: source closes, next stage's range ends, its defer closes, and so on to the sink
the runtime deadlock detector only fires when ALL goroutines are stuck, so in a real program the leak is silent — which is why the exercise tests guard waits with timeouts

questions.prompt: What does select do when several cases are ready at once? What does adding a default case change? And how did Counter use select to become stoppable?
expected_points: several ready cases: select picks one uniformly at random — never top-to-bottom priority
default runs immediately when no case is ready, making the select non-blocking — that is TryRecv
Counter selects between sending the next number and receiving from done; close(done) makes that case ready forever, so the goroutine returns and closes its output
close as broadcast: one close releases every goroutine selecting on done

questions.prompt: In MergeTwo, why set an exhausted input channel to nil instead of just leaving it in the select?
expected_points: a closed channel is always ready, yielding zero values — left in place, the select spins on it or forwards garbage
a nil channel is never ready, so its case goes dormant and the select waits on the remaining input alone
outside select, any send or receive on a nil channel blocks forever — a hang, not an error
the loop exits and closes the output once both inputs are nil

questions.prompt: You send a pointer to a struct through a channel and the receiving goroutine mutates the struct. Is that a data race? What is the rule?
expected_points: not a race if the sender stops using the value after sending — a channel send happens-before the corresponding receive completes
the idiom is ownership transfer: communicate the value instead of sharing it
if the sender keeps mutating after the send, it IS a race, and go test -race will flag it
